meaning: The speaker wants to do something. In questions, it asks what the listener wants to do.
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + たい (conjugates like an i-adjective)

senses.label: Want to (desire)
senses.meaning: The speaker wants to do something. Use it only for yourself, or in questions to the listener. For someone else's wishes, switch to 「〜たがる」 or 「〜たいと言っている」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + たい (行きます→行きたい; 食べます→食べたい; します→したい)
examples: I want to go to Hokkaido over summer vacation.
I want some cold water.
What do you want to eat?

senses.label: Don't want to
senses.meaning: 「〜たくない」 means you don't want to do something. It often signals lack of interest or a refusal. Polite forms: 「〜たくないです」 or 「〜たくありません」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + たくない／たくないです／たくありません
examples: I don't feel like going anywhere today.
I don't want to see that person.

senses.label: Wanted to
senses.meaning: 「〜たかった」 is a past wish. It often carries regret: you wanted to, but it didn't happen.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + たかった／たかったです
examples: When I was a kid, I wanted to be a pilot.
I really wish we could have talked longer.

senses.label: Want to try / aspirations
senses.meaning: After 「〜てみる」, it means you'd like to try something once. 「〜たいと思っています」 and 「〜たいと考えています」 are softer and more formal than plain 「〜たい」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + みたい; verb masu-stem + たいと思う／たいと考える
examples: I've always wanted to try authentic ramen at least once.
In the future, I'd like to work for a Japanese company.

notes: 「〜たい」 states only your own wishes directly (or asks the listener about theirs in a question). For a third person, use 「〜たがっている」 or 「〜たいと言っている」: ✕「田中さんは帰りたい」 → ○「田中さんは帰りたがっている」.
Asking a superior or a client 「〜たいですか」 directly (e.g. 「コーヒー、飲みたいですか」) sounds like you're prying into their personal desires, which is rude. Ask 「コーヒーはいかがですか」 or 「何になさいますか」 instead.
When making a request to a superior, a bare 「休みたいです」 sounds childish and too blunt. At work, say 「休みを取りたいのですが…」 or 「〜させていただきたいのですが」.
「〜たい」 conjugates like an i-adjective, so it can't take 「じゃない」 or 「でした」: ✕「行きたいじゃない」 → ○「行きたくない」; ✕「行きたいでした」 → ○「行きたかったです」.

daily.title: Deciding what to eat with a friend
daily.description: Between friends, plain form is the natural way to ask what someone wants.
daily.example: What do you want to eat today? — I kind of want ramen.

daily.title: Talking about vacation plans
daily.description: Adding 「なあ」 at the end makes a personal wish sound natural.
daily.example: I'd love to go to Okinawa this summer.

daily.title: Too tired to go out
daily.description: The negative form gently turns down an invitation or shows you're not in the mood.
daily.example: I'm tired, so I don't want to go anywhere today.

work.title: Stating your goals in a job interview
work.description: In formal settings, 「〜たいと考えております」 sounds composed and serious.
work.example: I would like to take on marketing work at your company.

work.title: Asking your boss for a day off
work.description: 「〜たいのですが」 states your wish politely and indirectly.
work.example: I was hoping to take next Friday off...

etymology: 「たい」 comes from 「たし」, a Classical Japanese auxiliary of desire. Its attributive form 「たき」 became 「たい」 through i-onbin (a sound change to い), and it later replaced the conclusive form as the modern form. 「たし」 appeared around the late Heian period. From the Kamakura period on, it replaced the older 「まほし」. One theory links it to the adjective 「いたし」 (甚し, “extreme”), but this is not settled. Because it began as an adjective-type auxiliary, 「たい」 still conjugates like an i-adjective.
formation: 「〜たい」 = verb masu-stem (the continuative form) + the desiderative auxiliary 「たい」. The continuative form is the shape a verb takes when something attaches to it, hence 「行き＋たい」 and 「食べ＋たい」. 「たい」 comes from the adjective-type auxiliary 「たし」, so it behaves like an i-adjective: like 「うれしい」 or 「ほしい」, it describes the speaker's inner feeling. As a result, 「行きたい」 as a whole becomes an adjective and conjugates like one (「たくない」／「たかった」). And because it describes an inner feeling, it can in principle only be said directly about yourself; other people's feelings can't be seen, so you add 「がる」 or 「そうだ」 to describe their outward signs. For the same reason, the object can be marked with 「が」 as the target of the feeling (「水が飲みたい」).

similar.title: 〜がほしい
similar.explanation: 「ほしい」 follows a noun and means wanting a thing; 「〜たい」 follows a verb and means wanting to do an action. Wanting a car: 「車がほしい」; wanting to buy a car: 「車を買いたい」, not ✕「車を買いほしい」.

similar.title: 〜たがる
similar.explanation: Same origin: the stem 「た」 of 「たい」 plus 「がる」 ("to show signs of"). It is reserved for a third person's wishes: 「弟はゲームを買いたがっている」. Use 「〜たい」 for yourself and 「〜たがる」 for others.

similar.title: 〜てほしい・〜てもらいたい
similar.explanation: 「〜たい」 is what you want to do; 「〜てほしい」 is what you want someone else to do. 「早く帰りたい」 (I want to go home early) vs 「早く帰ってほしい」 (I want you to go home early): the person doing the action is completely different.

similar.title: 〜つもりだ
similar.explanation: 「〜たい」 is just a wish and may never happen; 「つもり」 means you already intend or plan to do it. 「行きたい」 (I want to go) ≠ 「行くつもりだ」 (I plan to go). The connection also differs: 「つもり」 follows the dictionary form.

meaning: “Please do ...” Politely asks, instructs, or invites someone to do something.

senses.label: Asking for help
senses.meaning: Politely asks someone to do something for you. Used with shop staff, strangers, and coworkers. It is softer than a command, but the listener has little room to say no.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + ください (待つ→待ってください; 読む→読んでください)
examples: Excuse me, could you wait a moment, please?
Please speak a little more slowly.

senses.label: Instructions
senses.meaning: Teachers, doctors, and manuals use it to give directions and cautions. Polite but clear: “Do it this way.”
senses.connection: Verb te-form + ください
examples: Please open your textbooks to page 30.
Please take this medicine after meals.

senses.label: Offers and invitations
senses.meaning: Often paired with 「どうぞ」 to warmly invite someone to eat, sit, come in, and so on. It's kindness, not an order.
senses.connection: どうぞ + verb te-form + ください
examples: Please, help yourself to plenty.
Please, have a seat over here.

senses.label: More polite request
senses.meaning: 「〜てくださいませんか」 is phrased as a question. It leaves the listener room to refuse, so it is more polite than 「〜てください」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + くださいませんか／くださいますか
examples: Would you mind writing your name here?

notes: Even though it contains 「ください」, 「〜てください」 is still an instruction or demand. Using it to ask a superior or client for help sounds like you're giving orders; use 「〜ていただけますか」 or 「〜ていただけないでしょうか」 instead.
「ください」 directly after a noun asks for a thing (「水をください」); after a verb it must use the te-form: ✕「書きください」 → ○「書いてください」／「お書きください」.
Te-form sound changes are the most common error. 「行く」 is irregular: ✕「行いてください」 → ○「行ってください」. Verbs ending in む・ぶ・ぬ become 「んで」, and ぐ becomes 「いで」: 「読んでください」, 「急いでください」.
To ask someone not to do something, use 「〜ないでください」, not ✕「〜なくてください」.

daily.title: Asking a passerby to take a photo
daily.description: The go-to phrase for asking a stranger a small favor.
daily.example: Excuse me, could you take a picture for us?

daily.title: Welcoming a guest inside
daily.description: The host warmly invites a visitor to come in.
daily.example: Please, come on in.

daily.title: Didn't catch it on the phone
daily.description: Asking the other person to repeat what they said.
daily.example: Sorry, could you say that again?

work.title: A teacher in class
work.description: A teacher gives students instructions, politely but clearly.
work.example: Everyone, please open your textbooks.

work.title: Giving a coworker a task
work.description: Fine with coworkers or juniors. With a superior, switch to 「〜ていただけますか」.
work.example: Please make 10 copies of this document.

etymology: 「ください」 is the imperative of the verb 「くださる」 (下さる). 「くださる」 comes from 「くだす」 (下す, originally "to hand down from above, to bestow") plus the honorific auxiliary 「る」, meaning "a superior bestows something on an inferior". Its imperative was originally 「くだされ」, which changed to 「ください」 from the Edo period onward. Literally, 「〜てください」 means "please bestow on me the favor of (doing this action)", which gives it its polite tone; but since it is still formally an imperative, people often switch to softer forms such as 「〜ていただけますか」 with superiors.
formation: 「〜てください」 = verb te-form + 「ください」. 「ください」 is the imperative of the honorific verb 「くださる」 (a superior gives something to my side), so the whole phrase literally means "please bestow on me the action of doing...": the speaker is the one receiving the favor and the listener is the one granting it, which is why it expresses a request. But its backbone is still an imperative, and at its core it still means "make the other person do it". That's why it carries a sense of instruction when used to superiors; only by turning it into a question, 「〜ていただけますか」, and leaving the decision to the listener does it become a truly soft request.

similar.title: 〜をください
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「ください」, the imperative of 「くださる」. Noun + をください asks for a thing; te-form + ください asks for an action: 「水をください」 (Water, please) vs 「水を入れてください」 (Please pour some water).

similar.title: お〜ください
similar.explanation: Also ends in 「ください」, but is preceded by お + masu-stem. It is an honorific form used toward customers, common in shops, announcements and signs: 「お待ちください」, 「ご覧ください」. More respectful than 「待ってください」.

similar.title: 〜ていただけませんか
similar.explanation: A request phrased as a question, leaving the decision to the listener, so it is far softer than 「〜てください」. It is the first choice when asking a superior or client: 「確認していただけませんか」.

similar.title: 〜なさい
similar.explanation: Also tells someone to do something, but 「〜なさい」 is a command from above to below (parent to child, teacher to student) and can't be used to equals or superiors. 「〜てください」 is a polite request or instruction.

meaning: “Please don't ...” Politely forbids or discourages something, or tells someone they needn't do it.

senses.label: Polite prohibition
senses.meaning: Asks someone not to do something. Common on signs, in announcements, and in reminders. It is softer than 「〜てはいけない」: a request from the speaker, not a rule.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + でください (吸う→吸わないでください; 触る→触らないでください)
examples: Please don't smoke here.
Please do not touch the artwork.

senses.label: Reassurance and care
senses.meaning: Tells someone not to worry, not to mind, or not to push themselves. It shows concern for the listener.
senses.connection: 心配する／気にする／無理する, etc. + ないでください
examples: Please don't worry. It's fine.
Don't overdo it, okay?

senses.label: Reminders
senses.meaning: Reminds someone not to forget, not to be late, and so on. Adding 「ね」 makes it warmer.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + でください(ね)
examples: Don't forget our plans tomorrow, okay?
Please don't be late tomorrow.

notes: It's 「ないで」, not 「なくて」: ✕「触らなくてください」 → ○「触らないでください」. (「なくて」 is used in 「〜なくてもいい」.)
「〜ないでください」 is still a prohibition and sounds rather blunt to customers and superiors. More tactful forms for customers are 「〜はご遠慮ください」 and 「〜ないでいただけますか」; signs often say 「お手を触れないでください」.
Among friends you can shorten it to 「〜ないで」 or 「〜ないでね」, but this is very casual; dropping 「ください」 at work sounds rude.

daily.title: Visiting a sick friend
daily.description: Friends comfort each other and usually drop 「ください」.
daily.example: Don't worry, okay? You'll get better soon.

daily.title: Saying goodbye to a partner
daily.description: Close people simply say 「〜ないで」.
daily.example: Don't cry. We'll see each other again.

daily.title: A sign in the park
daily.description: Signs in public places often use this polite prohibition.
daily.example: Please keep off the grass.

work.title: Reminding a coworker before a meeting
work.description: Reminding someone to be on time.
work.example: Please don't be late for tomorrow's meeting.

work.title: An internal company notice
work.description: Office rules stated in a polite tone.
work.example: Please do not take equipment out of the meeting room.

etymology: 「ないで」 consists of the negative auxiliary 「ない」 and the conjunctive particle 「で」. It is generally thought that the negative auxiliary 「ない」 spread in the Kanto (Edo) dialect during the Edo period; before that, Classical Japanese 「ず」 was widely used, and "without doing ... and ..." was usually expressed as 「〜ずに」 or 「〜ずして」. 「ないで」 developed in Edo speech along with it. 「ください」 is the imperative of 「くださる（下さる）」 (see 〜てください). So 「〜ないでください」 literally means "please bestow on me the favor of not doing ...".
formation: 「〜ないでください」 = negative 「ない」 + particle 「で」 + 「ください」. 「〜ないで」 means "in a state of not doing...", and adding 「ください」 (please grant me the favor of...) gives "please act toward me by not doing...", that is, "please don't...". The reason it uses 「ないで」 and not 「なくて」 is that 「ないで」 expresses the manner or state of an action (「傘を持たないで出かける」), while 「なくて」 mainly expresses cause or coordination (「お金がなくて困る」). Asking someone to act in a way that involves not doing something requires 「ないで」, the form that expresses manner.

similar.title: 〜てはいけない
similar.explanation: Both express prohibition. 「〜ないでください」 politely asks the listener not to do something; 「〜てはいけません」 announces that something isn't allowed by rule or principle, which sounds condescending to customers or superiors.

similar.title: 〜な (prohibition)
similar.explanation: Dictionary form + な (「触るな」) is the harshest prohibition, used on signs, in men's casual speech or when scolding; 「〜ないでください」 is a polite request. Saying 「〜な」 to someone's face is very rude.

similar.title: 〜ないで (without doing)
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are built from the negative 「ない」 + 「で」. Followed by an ordinary verb, 「〜ないで」 means "do B without doing A" (「朝ご飯を食べないで出かけた」); only when followed by 「ください」 does it ask someone not to do something.

meaning: Shows an action in progress or a resulting state that continues. It can also express habits or past experience.
connection: Verb te-form + いる (casual: 〜てる／〜でる; humble-polite: 〜ております)

senses.label: In progress
senses.meaning: With verbs that describe ongoing activity (読む, 食べる, 降る), 「ている」 means the action is happening now, like English “-ing”.
senses.connection: Durative verb te-form + いる
examples: It's raining now.
What are you doing? — Watching TV.
The kids are playing in the park.

senses.label: Resulting state
senses.meaning: With instantaneous change verbs (開く, 結婚する, 知る), 「ている」 shows the state left after the change. 「窓が開いている」 doesn't mean “is opening”; it means “is open”.
senses.connection: Change-of-state verb te-form + いる (also common with wearing verbs like 着る and かける)
examples: The window is open.
My older sister is already married.
The person wearing glasses is Mr. Tanaka.

senses.label: Habits and jobs
senses.meaning: Things done repeatedly over a long period, or someone's current job or status. Often used with 「毎朝」 or 「いつも」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + いる (often with 「毎日」 or 「いつも」)
examples: I go jogging every morning.
My older brother works for a company in Tokyo.

senses.label: Experience and record
senses.meaning: Presents a past event as part of someone's experience or record today. Common in résumés and news reports.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + いる
examples: My father studied in America when he was young.
She has won this tournament twice before.

notes: Instantaneous verbs (「結婚する」, 「死ぬ」, 「来る」, 「着く」) + 「ている」 express a resulting state, not an ongoing action: 「結婚している」 = is married, not "is in the middle of a wedding"; 「来ている」 = has come (and is here now).
When asked 「もう食べましたか」, the negative answer is 「いいえ、まだ食べていません」; ✕「まだ食べませんでした」 means "I didn't eat (at that time)", not "I haven't eaten yet".
Answering a superior's reminder with 「わかっています」 sounds like "I already know, stop nagging", which is rude. Answer 「承知しました」, 「かしこまりました」 or 「はい、気をつけます」 instead.
「知る」: the affirmative is 「知っています」, but the negative is 「知りません／知らない」, not ✕「知っていません」.
The spoken contractions 「〜てる」 and 「〜でる」 are for casual situations only; in formal writing and when talking to superiors, use 「〜ています」 or 「〜ております」.

daily.title: Asking what someone's up to on the phone
daily.description: Friends usually shorten it to 「〜てる」.
daily.example: What are you doing right now? — Eating.

daily.title: Pointing out a family member
daily.description: The resulting-state use describes what someone is wearing.
daily.example: The person in the red clothes is my sister.

daily.title: Telling family about the weather
daily.description: Describing something happening right now.
daily.example: It's snowing outside!

work.title: Closing a business email
work.description: 「〜ております」 is the formal version.
work.example: I look forward to hearing from you.

work.title: Introducing your job
work.description: Explaining your current role.
work.example: I currently work in sales at an IT company.

etymology: 「いる」 was written 「ゐる」 (居る) in older Japanese and originally meant "to sit, to stay put somewhere". Classical Japanese used the auxiliaries 「たり」 and 「り」 to express the continuation or result of an action; from the medieval period on, 「〜てゐる」 (te-form + 居る) gradually developed and, in the modern era, became the main form for progressive and resultant states. Western Japan still widely uses 「〜とる／〜ておる」; 「おる」 (居る) was also originally a verb of existence, but in standard Japanese it became the humble or formal counterpart of 「いる」.
formation: 「〜ている」 = verb te-form + the existence verb 「いる」 (originally "to stay, to be there"). The te-form presents an action, and 「いる」 says "the subject stays in the situation created by that action". With durative verbs (「読む」, 「走る」) the action itself can continue, so "being inside the action" means it is in progress; with instantaneous verbs (「結婚する」, 「死ぬ」) the action is over in a moment, so "being after the action" means a resulting state. Stretch "being in..." over daily life and you get habits and occupations (「毎朝走っている」); stretch it over a whole life history and you get experiences and records. So all of its uses are really one structure: the subject is in the state formed by an action.

similar.title: 〜てある
similar.explanation: Both can express a resulting state. 「窓が開いている」 just describes the state; 「窓が開けてある」 implies someone deliberately opened it for a purpose and left it that way. 「〜てある」 takes transitive verbs, while result-state 「〜ている」 mostly takes intransitive verbs.

similar.title: 〜ところだ
similar.explanation: 「〜ているところだ」 stresses being right in the middle of an action at that moment, a clearer answer to "What are you doing now?": 「今、ご飯を食べているところです」. 「〜ている」 can also express habits and states; 「ところだ」 can't.

similar.title: 〜つつある
similar.explanation: A written form for a change progressing step by step (「景気は回復しつつある」). With change verbs, 「〜ている」 usually means the change is already complete (「回復している」 = has recovered); to say "is in the process of recovering", use 「〜つつある」.

similar.title: 〜まま
similar.explanation: Both can express a state that continues. 「〜たまま」 stresses that something stayed unchanged, often with a sense of "it shouldn't have" (「電気をつけたまま寝た」); 「〜ている」 describes the state neutrally.

meaning: Gives permission (“you may ...”) or asks for it. 「〜なくてもいい」 means “you don't have to”.
connection: Verb te-form + もいい; noun / na-adjective + でもいい; negative: 〜なくてもいい

senses.label: Permission
senses.meaning: Tells someone they may do something. Common from a superior to a junior, or from a host to a guest. Replacing 「いい」 with 「かまわない」 is more formal.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + もいい／もかまわない
examples: You can go home for today.
You may take photos here.

senses.label: Asking permission
senses.meaning: As a question, it means “May I ...?” More polite: 「〜てもよろしいでしょうか」. Reply with 「ええ、どうぞ」 or 「すみません、ちょっと…」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + もいいですか／もよろしいですか
examples: May I take pictures in this room?
Would it be all right if I sat here?

senses.label: Don't have to
senses.meaning: 「〜なくてもいい」 means it's fine not to do something; there's no need. It is the opposite of 「〜なければならない」 (must).
senses.connection: Verb nai-form (drop い) + くてもいい
examples: You don't have to pay right now.
You don't need to come tomorrow.

senses.label: Concession (that's fine too)
senses.meaning: Steps back: it isn't ideal, but it's acceptable. Often follows nouns and adjectives. It can also show willingness to go along with something.
senses.connection: Noun / na-adjective + でもいい; i-adjective 〜くて + もいい
examples: Would tomorrow be okay?
If it's cheap, I don't mind if it's old.
I can help you if you like.

notes: Saying 「〜てもいいですよ」 to a superior or client sounds like "I'll allow you to", which is condescending and very rude. To offer help, use 「〜ましょうか」: ✕「部長、手伝ってもいいですよ」 → ○「お手伝いしましょうか」.
When asking a superior or client for permission, 「〜てもいいですか」 is a bit casual; in formal settings use 「〜てもよろしいでしょうか」 or 「〜させていただいてもよろしいでしょうか」.
「〜なくてもいい」 means "don't have to", not "must not": 「来なくてもいい」 = you don't need to come. For "must not", use 「〜てはいけない」.
Among friends, 「手伝ってもいいよ」 suggests "I could help, I guess" (not especially eager). To sound willing, just say 「手伝うよ」.

daily.title: Using the bathroom at a friend's place
daily.description: Friends ask permission in plain form.
daily.example: Can I use your bathroom?

daily.title: Rescheduling with a friend
daily.description: 「でもいい」 offers a compromise.
daily.example: Is it okay if we meet at 4 instead?

daily.title: Telling family not to wait up
daily.description: Permission used as a kind gesture.
daily.example: I'll be late, so feel free to go to bed.

work.title: Asking a question in a meeting
work.description: Use 「よろしいでしょうか」 when asking a superior or client.
work.example: Excuse me, may I ask a quick question?

work.title: A boss says no overtime needed
work.description: 「〜なくてもいい」 means there's no need.
work.example: You don't need to work overtime today.

etymology: Made of the conjunctive particle 「て」 + the concessive particle 「も」 ("even if") + the adjective 「いい」. Literally "even if you do ..., it is good", which extended to permission. 「いい」 is a colloquial variant of 「よい」; it is generally thought that forms such as 「えい」 and 「いい」 became popular in speech from the Edo period onward, while written language still mostly uses 「よい」. That is why its conjugations (よかった, よければ) are still based on 「よい」.
formation: 「〜てもいい」 = te-form + the concessive particle 「も」 (even if) + the evaluative word 「いい」 (good, OK). Literally: "even if you do..., it's fine". Stating that doing it is fine gives permission; asking "is it fine if I do it?" asks for permission; and with the negative 「なくて」 in front it becomes "it's fine even if you don't" = you don't have to. Because at its core it judges an action as acceptable, the speaker takes the position of the one evaluating and approving, which is why saying 「〜てもいいですよ」 to a superior sounds like you are "approving" them.

similar.title: 〜てもかまわない
similar.explanation: Same meaning as 「〜てもいい」 but more formal, with a concessive nuance of "I don't mind even if...": 「明日でもかまいません」.

similar.title: 〜なくてもいい
similar.explanation: Same origin: replace the first part with the negative 「〜なくて」 and it means "it's fine not to do" (don't have to). 「行ってもいい」 (you may go) vs 「行かなくてもいい」 (you don't have to go).

similar.title: 〜ても差し支えない
similar.explanation: Permission for written and formal settings, roughly "there is no problem if...", common in notices and business documents: 「鉛筆で書いても差し支えありません」. In everyday conversation, use 「〜てもいい」.

similar.title: 〜ても (even if)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the 「ても」 in 「〜てもいい」 is the concessive "even if". 「雨が降っても行く」 (I'll go even if it rains) is a plain concession; only by adding 「いい」 does it become "it's fine even if you do" = permission.

meaning: “You must not ...” Prohibition based on rules or common sense. It can also be a strong warning.
connection: Verb te-form + はいけない (casual: 〜ちゃいけない／〜じゃいけない)

senses.label: Rule-based prohibition
senses.meaning: States the rules of a school, company, or society. The tone is objective and clear. Polite form: 「〜てはいけません」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + はいけない／はいけません
examples: You may not use your phone during class.
Swimming is not allowed here.

senses.label: Casual prohibition
senses.meaning: Parents to children, or friends to each other, warning strongly. In speech it contracts to 「〜ちゃだめ」 or 「〜じゃだめ」, which sounds very direct.
senses.connection: ては→ちゃ, では→じゃ + いけない／だめ
examples: Don't play in the street!
You shouldn't eat that much.

senses.label: Formal prohibition
senses.meaning: 「〜てはならない」 appears in laws, maxims, and writing. It sounds solemn.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + はならない
examples: One must not steal what belongs to others.
We must never forget this failure.

senses.label: Asking for permission
senses.meaning: The negative question 「〜てはいけませんか」 means “Would it be a problem if ...?” It gently asks for permission.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + はいけませんか
examples: Would it be all right if I took tomorrow off?

notes: 「〜てはいけません」 announces a prohibition based on rules, so using it to customers or superiors sounds like a lecture. When asking outsiders not to do something, use 「〜ないでください」 or 「〜はご遠慮ください」.
Don't mistake 「〜なくてはいけない」 (must) for a prohibition; it means the exact opposite: 「食べなくてはいけない」 = you must eat, 「食べてはいけない」 = you must not eat.
The contractions 「ちゃ／じゃ」 follow the te-form: 「て」 → 「ちゃ」, 「で」 → 「じゃ」: 「飲んじゃいけない」, 「遊んじゃだめ」; not ✕「飲んちゃいけない」.

daily.title: A parent teaching a child
daily.description: The contracted form sounds stern.
daily.example: You must never go off with a stranger.

daily.title: Doctor's orders
daily.description: Explaining what you must observe for your health.
daily.example: You shouldn't take a bath today.

daily.title: A friend warning against drunk driving
daily.description: Friends warn each other directly.
daily.example: If you're driving, you can't drink.

work.title: New employee training
work.description: Explaining company rules in a neutral tone.
work.example: Do not share internal company information with outsiders.

work.title: Exam room rules
work.description: The proctor announces the rules.
work.example: Dictionaries may not be used during the exam.

etymology: 「いけない」 is the negative of the verb 「いける」 (行ける, "can go, works out"), originally meaning "cannot go, doesn't work", and by extension "no good, not allowed". 「〜ては」 = the conjunctive particle 「て」 + the topic particle 「は」, setting up a hypothetical condition: "if you do ..., it won't work", hence a prohibition. 「〜ちゃ」 and 「〜じゃ」 are contracted sound changes of 「ては」 and 「では」. In the written form 「〜てはならない」, 「ならない」 is the negative of 「成る」, meaning "won't hold, is not acceptable".
formation: 「〜てはいけない」 = verb te-form + topic particle 「は」 + 「いけない」. 「〜ては」 sets up a hypothetical condition, "if you do...", and 「いけない」 is the negative of 「行ける」 (to work out), meaning "won't work, no good". Together: "if you do..., it won't do" → prohibition. The parts of this "condition + negative evaluation" frame can be swapped: replace 「いけない」 with 「ならない」 and you get the written 「〜てはならない」; replace it with 「だめ」 and you get the casual 「〜てはだめ」. Change the condition to the negative 「なくては」 (if you don't), and "not doing it won't do" becomes "must". This is why 「〜てはいけない」 and 「〜なくてはいけない」 look so similar yet mean opposite things.

similar.title: 〜てはならない
similar.explanation: Same origin and meaning, used in writing, laws and admonitions. It sounds more solemn and absolute than 「いけない」 (「人の物を盗んではならない」) and is rarely used in everyday conversation.

similar.title: 〜ないでください
similar.explanation: Both express prohibition. 「〜てはいけない」 states a rule; 「〜ないでください」 asks the listener not to do something and is more polite, so choose it for customers and superiors.

similar.title: 〜な (prohibition)
similar.explanation: 「〜な」 is an imperative prohibition and extremely blunt, mostly seen on signs, in men's casual speech or when scolding (「入るな」); 「〜てはいけない」 states a rule and is less aggressive.

similar.title: 〜べきではない
similar.explanation: 「〜べきではない」 argues from morality or common sense that something "shouldn't" be done and carries the speaker's personal judgment (「人の悪口を言うべきではない」); 「〜てはいけない」 usually means something isn't allowed by rules.

meaning: “Must / have to.” Expresses obligation or necessity: not doing it is not an option.
connection: Verb nai-form (drop い) + ければならない／くてはいけない; verb nai-form + といけない

senses.label: Duty and rules
senses.meaning: Social rules or objective obligations. 「〜なければならない」 leans formal. Polite form: 「〜なければなりません」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form (drop い) + ければならない／ければなりません
examples: In Japan, cars must drive on the left.
Environmental problems must be addressed by the whole world.

senses.label: Personal necessity
senses.meaning: Something you have to do in a specific situation. 「〜なくてはいけない」 and 「〜ないといけない」 sound more conversational.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form (drop い) + くてはいけない; verb nai-form + といけない
examples: I have to get up early tomorrow.
You have to take the medicine every day.

senses.label: Casual contractions
senses.meaning: In everyday speech it shrinks to 「〜なきゃ」 or 「〜なくちゃ」, and the rest is often dropped. Common when talking to yourself or excusing yourself.
senses.connection: なければ→なきゃ; なくては→なくちゃ
examples: Oh, look at the time. I've got to go home.
I need to write my report.

senses.label: Must be ...
senses.meaning: After nouns or adjectives, it means “has to be ...” and states a requirement.
senses.connection: i-adjective 〜く + なければならない; noun / na-adjective + でなければならない
examples: Answers must be accurate.
The classroom needs to be brighter.

notes: "Don't have to" is 「〜なくてもいい」, not ✕「なければならなくない」.
Saying 「〜なければなりません」 to a superior or client forces an obligation on them and sounds like an order. To ask them to do something, use 「〜ていただけますか」 or 「〜ていただく必要がございます」.
「〜なきゃ」 and 「〜なくちゃ」 are only for friends and family; in business settings you must use the full forms 「〜なければなりません」 or 「〜なくてはいけません」.
A common connection error: drop 「い」 from the nai-form and add 「ければ」: 「行かない」→「行かなければ」, 「しない」→「しなければ」, not ✕「するなければ」. Adjectives: 「高くなければ」; nouns: 「学生でなければ」.

daily.title: Leaving a party early
daily.description: Friends use the contracted form and drop the ending.
daily.example: Sorry, I have an early start tomorrow, so I've got to head home.

daily.title: Suddenly remembering to buy something
daily.description: Reminding yourself out loud.
daily.example: Oh, I need to buy milk.

daily.title: After seeing the doctor
daily.description: Explaining something you personally have to do.
daily.example: The doctor told me to, so I have to take medicine every day.

work.title: Reminding someone of a deadline
work.description: A work obligation stated in formal polite speech.
work.example: The report must be submitted by Friday.

work.title: Explaining company rules
work.description: Stating a rule objectively.
work.example: You must show your employee ID when entering the building.

etymology: 「なければ」 is the hypothetical form 「なけれ」 of the negative auxiliary 「ない」 + the conjunctive particle 「ば」 ("if not ..."), and 「ならない」 is the negative of the verb 「なる」 (成る, "to hold, to work out"). Literally, "if you don't do ..., it won't work" — a double negative expressing "must". 「なくては〜」 works the same way ("if you don't, then ..."). The colloquial 「なきゃ」 is a further contraction of 「なけりゃ」 (a sound change of なければ), and 「なくちゃ」 is a sound change of 「なくては」.
formation: 「〜なければならない」 = 「なけれ」, the hypothetical form of the negative 「ない」 + conditional 「ば」 (if not...) + 「ならない」, the negative of 「なる」 (won't do). Literally: "if you don't do..., it won't do". The two negatives block off the option of "not doing", leaving only "doing": this is the logic of a double negative meaning "must". The first half, "if you don't", can be swapped for 「なくては」 or 「ないと」, and the second half, "won't do", for 「いけない」 or 「だめ」, producing a whole family of synonymous forms. In speech the second half is often dropped, leaving just 「なきゃ」 or 「なくちゃ」, and the listener naturally fills in "or it won't do".

similar.title: 〜ないといけない
similar.explanation: Same meaning but more conversational, often used for the speaker's own specific situation (「もう帰らないといけない」); 「〜なければならない」 is more formal and objective, suited to rules and writing.

similar.title: 〜なくちゃ・〜なきゃ
similar.explanation: Spoken contractions of the same origin (「なくては」→「なくちゃ」, 「なければ」→「なきゃ」). They often drop the second half 「いけない」 and are only used in close relationships.

similar.title: 〜べきだ
similar.explanation: 「〜べきだ」 is the speaker arguing from reason or morality that something "should" be done, with a strong personal tone; 「〜なければならない」 focuses on objective obligation or necessity. Laws use 「なければならない」; personal opinions use 「べきだ」.

similar.title: 〜ざるを得ない
similar.explanation: Also uses a double negative to mean "have no choice but to", but stresses "I didn't want to, but circumstances forced me", and is rather literary; 「〜なければならない」 simply states an obligation without necessarily implying reluctance.

meaning: “Let's ...” Invites someone to do something together, or offers to do something for them.
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + ましょう／ましょうか

senses.label: Let's do it together
senses.meaning: Invites the listener to do something with you. The tone is upbeat and assumes they'll agree. It is the polite version of 「〜(よ)う」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + ましょう (行きます→行きましょう; 休みます→休みましょう)
examples: Let's take a break soon.
Let's go home together.

senses.label: Offering help
senses.meaning: 「〜ましょうか」 offers “Shall I ...?” It asks whether the listener would like your help.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + ましょうか
examples: That looks heavy. Shall I carry it?
Shall I open the window?

senses.label: Consulting (shall we?)
senses.meaning: 「〜ましょうか」 also discusses what to do together. It shows more respect for the other person's opinion than 「〜ましょう」.
senses.connection: Question word / verb masu-stem + ましょうか
examples: Where shall we meet?
Shall we take a short break?

senses.label: Calls to action
senses.meaning: Textbooks, notices, and slogans use it to give gentle instructions to everyone.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + ましょう
examples: Now, let's read the textbook.
Please put out your garbage on the designated days.

notes: 「〜ましょう」 pushes an action forward on the assumption that the listener will agree. In a first invitation (especially to a superior), saying 「行きましょう」 straight away sounds like you're deciding for them; first ask about their wishes with 「〜ませんか」.
「〜ましょうか」 has two meanings with different subjects: 「持ちましょうか」 = shall I carry it for you?; 「行きましょうか」 = shall we go? Don't mistake an offer of help for an invitation to do something together.
When offering help to a superior, 「〜ましょうか」 is a little casual; the more respectful humble forms are 「お持ちしましょうか」 and 「お調べいたしましょうか」.
「〜ましょう」 expresses will and can't be used for guesses: ✕「明日は雨が降りましょう」 → ○「明日は雨が降るでしょう」.

daily.title: Deciding to eat with a friend
daily.description: Suggesting you do something together.
daily.example: I'm hungry. Let's get something to eat.

daily.title: Helping an elderly person with luggage
daily.description: Offering help with humble language sounds even more polite.
daily.example: May I carry your bags for you?

daily.title: Cheering each other on during a hike
daily.description: Encouraging everyone to keep going.
daily.example: We're almost there. Let's keep going!

work.title: Chairing a meeting
work.description: Announcing the start and rallying everyone.
work.example: It's time, so let's begin the meeting.

work.title: Dividing tasks with a coworker
work.description: Volunteering to take on a task.
work.example: Shall I prepare the materials?

etymology: 「ましょう」 consists of 「ませ」, the irrealis form of the polite auxiliary 「ます」, and the conjectural/volitional auxiliary 「う」. 「う」 comes from Classical Japanese 「む」, which changed via 「ん」 to 「う」. 「ませう」 then became 「ましょう」 through palatalization. 「ます」 itself is generally thought to have evolved from 「まゐらす」 (参らす, a humble verb of offering) via 「まらする」 and 「まする」, becoming the ordinary polite auxiliary from the Edo period onward.
formation: 「〜ましょう」 = 「ませ」, the irrealis form of the polite auxiliary 「ます」 + the volitional auxiliary 「う」 (「ませう」 → 「ましょう」). 「う」 expresses the speaker's will (plain 「行こう」 = I'll go / let's go), and adding 「ます」 makes it polite. When the speaker voices their own will and the listener is included among those acting, it becomes "let's do it together"; add the question 「か」 to hand that will over to the listener for confirmation, and it becomes a consultation or "shall I do it?". Because its core is the speaker's "will", it can't be used for things unrelated to will, such as the weather or other people's actions.

similar.title: 〜ませんか
similar.explanation: Both can be used for invitations. 「〜ませんか」 uses a negative question to ask the listener's wishes first, leaving room to decline; 「〜ましょう」 pushes a joint action assuming the listener will agree. Usually you ask with 「〜ませんか」 first, then say 「〜ましょう」 once they agree.

similar.title: 〜ましょうか (suggestion / offer)
similar.explanation: Same origin: adding the question 「か」 to 「ましょう」 hands the speaker's will over to the listener for confirmation. It can be used to consult (「何時に会いましょうか」) or to offer help (「手伝いましょうか」).

similar.title: 〜(よ)う (volitional form)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the plain form of 「ましょう」 is the volitional 「〜(よ)う」 (「行こう」, 「食べよう」); friends say 「一緒に行こう」. To elders and superiors, use 「〜ましょう」.

meaning: “Won't you ...? / Would you like to ...?” A polite invitation phrased as a negative question.
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + ませんか

senses.label: Inviting someone
senses.meaning: The “won't you ...?” form leaves the decision to the listener. It shows more respect than 「〜ましょう」 and is the most common polite invitation.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + ませんか (often with 「一緒に」, 「よかったら」, or 「今度」)
examples: Would you like to play tennis together this weekend?
If you'd like, why not come over to my place sometime?

senses.label: Offering refreshments
senses.meaning: A polite way to offer food, drink, or a rest. It often comes with 「〜でも」, which keeps it casual and low-pressure.
senses.connection: (Noun + でも) + verb masu-stem + ませんか
examples: Would you like some tea or something?
Shall we take a little break?

notes: 「〜ませんか」 invites the listener to do something; to ask someone to do something for you, use 「〜てくれませんか」 or 「〜ていただけませんか」. 「手伝いませんか」 means "Would you like to join in helping?"; to ask for help, say 「手伝っていただけませんか」.
Answering an invitation with a flat 「いいえ、行きません」 is very rude. Say 「すみません、その日はちょっと…」 or 「行きたいんですが、用事があって…」, declining softly with a half-finished sentence.
「わかりませんか」, 「ありませんか」 and the like are ordinary negative questions ("Don't you understand?", "Isn't there any?"), not invitations; tell them apart by the verb and the context.
When inviting a superior, 「〜ませんか」 is not quite respectful enough; use the honorific 「〜にいらっしゃいませんか」 or 「ご一緒にいかがですか」.

daily.title: Inviting a friend to a movie
daily.description: A polite invitation that lets the other person decide.
daily.example: Want to go see a movie on Saturday?

daily.title: Inviting a neighbor
daily.description: The most tactful choice with someone you don't know well yet.
daily.example: Would you like to have tea together sometime?

daily.title: Taking a photo with a travel companion
daily.description: A casual suggestion on the spot.
daily.example: Shall we take a picture together here?

work.title: Inviting a coworker to lunch
work.description: A polite invitation between colleagues.
work.example: Tanaka-san, would you like to have lunch together?

work.title: Suggesting a break in a meeting
work.description: A suggestion framed as a question.
work.example: Shall we take a short break?

etymology: 「ません」 is 「ませ」, the irrealis form of the polite auxiliary 「ます」, plus the negative auxiliary 「ぬ」 (which changed to 「ん」). The final 「か」 is the question particle. Inviting through a negative question is a common indirect strategy in Japanese: instead of saying "let's go", you ask "won't you go?", leaving the other person room to say no.
formation: 「〜ませんか」 = 「ません」, the negative of the polite 「ます」 + the question particle 「か」. Literally: "Won't you do...?". By asking in the negative, the speaker doesn't decide for the listener; they simply put the possibility of doing it on the table and ask the listener to respond, while leaving room to say 「いいえ」. This is the logic of the soft Japanese invitation: instead of saying "Let's go", you ask "Won't you go?". The same structure in plain speech is 「〜ない？」 with rising intonation.

similar.title: 〜ましょう
similar.explanation: In invitations, 「〜ませんか」 first asks the listener's wishes; 「〜ましょう」 pushes the action forward assuming they'll agree, and is often used to accept an invitation: 「ええ、行きましょう」.

similar.title: 〜ましょうか (suggestion / offer)
similar.explanation: 「〜ましょうか」 is "Shall we...?", a consultation that already assumes you'll do it together and only discusses details or timing; 「〜ませんか」 starts by asking whether to do it at all, so it is more polite.

similar.title: 〜ない？ (invitation)
similar.explanation: The plain form of 「〜ませんか」, said among friends with rising intonation: 「一緒に帰らない？」. To superiors or people you've just met, use 「〜ませんか」.

similar.title: 〜はどうですか・〜はいかがですか
similar.explanation: Both can offer something or suggest trying it. 「お茶はいかがですか」 puts the item right in front of the listener to choose and is more respectful; 「お茶でも飲みませんか」 invites the listener to do an action together.

meaning: Lists a few representative actions (“do things like A and B”), or shows actions or states alternating back and forth.
connection: Verb ta-form + り, verb ta-form + り + する

senses.label: Listing examples
senses.meaning: Picks a few examples from many activities, implying there are others. It says nothing about order. The final 「する」 closes the list and carries the tense.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + り, verb ta-form + り + する (読んだり、聞いたり)
examples: On my days off, I read books, listen to music, that kind of thing.
Over the weekend I did some cleaning and laundry.

senses.label: Back and forth
senses.meaning: Two opposite actions alternate, like “back and forth” or “on and off”.
senses.connection: Two opposite verbs in ta-form + り + する
examples: He is pacing back and forth in the room.
The light keeps flickering on and off.

senses.label: Changing states
senses.meaning: With adjectives or nouns, it shows a state that keeps changing, sometimes one way, sometimes the other.
senses.connection: i-adjective 〜かったり; noun / na-adjective 〜だったり; verbs also possible
examples: Lately it's been hot one day and cold the next.
The weather is alternating between sunny and cloudy.

senses.label: Softened example
senses.meaning: A single 「〜たりする」 gives one example softly, like “or anything like that”. Common in reminders and when talking about habits.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + り + する／しない
examples: Please don't do things like sleeping in class.
Now and then I go see a movie on my own.

notes: When listing two actions, both take 「たり」, and 「する」 comes at the end: ✕「本を読んだり、音楽を聞きます」 → ○「本を読んだり、音楽を聞いたりします」.
「〜たり〜たり」 just picks a few examples with no order; to narrate in sequence ("first..., then..."), use 「〜て、〜て」: ○「起きて、顔を洗って、学校へ行った」.
Tense and politeness appear only on the final 「する」: ○「行ったり来たりしました」, not ✕「行きましたり来ましたりする」.

daily.title: Chatting about the weekend
daily.description: Giving examples of what you did.
daily.example: On Sunday I did some shopping and met up with friends.

daily.title: Reacting to a movie
daily.description: Two opposite emotions alternating.
daily.example: That movie had me crying and laughing.

daily.title: Sharing travel stories
daily.description: Listing activities from a trip.
daily.example: In Kyoto I visited temples, drank matcha, and so on.

work.title: Talking about hobbies in an interview
work.description: Giving examples and hinting there's more.
work.example: On my days off, I go jogging, read books, things like that.

work.title: A reminder from your boss
work.description: A gentle warning using one example.
work.example: Please don't be looking at your phones during meetings.

etymology: 「たり」 comes from the Classical Japanese perfective/continuative auxiliary 「たり」, which is itself a contraction of 「て」 + 「あり」 (てあり→たり). From the medieval period on, 「〜たり〜たり」 was used to list two or more actions, gradually developing into the modern listing use. The modern past auxiliary 「た」 also arose from 「たる」, the attributive form of 「たり」, losing its final syllable; so 「たり」 and 「た」 share the same origin, and both show the same voicing in 「〜んだり」 and 「〜いだり」.
formation: 「たり」 comes from the classical auxiliary 「たり」 (a contraction of 「て」 + 「あり」) and shares its origin with the past auxiliary 「た」, so it attaches exactly as 「た」 does (「読んだり」, 「来たり」). Each 「〜たり」 means "doing things like..."; you line up several such actions and then use 「する」 to bundle them into one predicate, with 「する」 meaning roughly "do (this sort of thing)". Because it only lines up a few examples, there is no time order, and it hints that there are others; pair two opposite actions (「行ったり来たり」) and it shows alternation. Tense and politeness are carried by the final 「する」.

similar.title: 〜て (te-form linking / sequence)
similar.explanation: 「〜て、〜て」 lists actions completely and in time order; 「〜たり〜たり」 picks only a few representative actions out of many, in no order, and implies there are others.

similar.title: 〜とか〜とか
similar.explanation: Also lists examples, but more conversational and casual, and can take nouns as well as verbs (「映画を見るとか、買い物するとか」); 「〜たり〜たり」 takes verbs and adjectives and ends with 「する」.

similar.title: 〜や〜など
similar.explanation: 「〜や〜など」 gives representative nouns (「りんごやバナナなど」); to give representative actions, switch to 「〜たり〜たりする」.

similar.title: 〜たりして
similar.explanation: Same origin: a single 「〜たり」 + 「して」, used in speech for vague examples or half-joking guesses (「もしかして、彼が犯人だったりして」).

meaning: “Have done ... before.” Expresses past experience. The negative means “have never ...”.
connection: Verb ta-form + ことがある／ことがない

senses.label: Have done before
senses.meaning: Something you have experienced in your life, usually notable or out of the ordinary. Not for recent everyday events like “I went to the supermarket yesterday”.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ことがある (polite: 〜たことがあります; 「が」 is often dropped in speech)
examples: Have you ever been to Japan?
I have worked in China.
Have you read that book?

senses.label: Have never done
senses.meaning: The negative 「〜たことがない」 means you've never done it. 「一度も」 or 「まだ」 often add emphasis.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ことがない／ことがありません
examples: I have never once eaten natto.
I still haven't climbed Mt. Fuji.

senses.label: Emphasizing rarity
senses.meaning: 「こんな〜は〜たことがない」 means “I've never seen anything like it”. It stresses how extreme something is.
senses.connection: こんな／これほど + noun + は + verb ta-form + ことがない
examples: I've never seen such beautiful scenery.
I've never had such a delicious cake.

notes: One 「た」 makes all the difference: 「行ったことがある」 = have been (experience); 「行くことがある」 = sometimes go (frequency).
「〜たことがある」 describes an experience worth mentioning, at some distance in time. It can't be used for recent, everyday things: ✕「昨日、ご飯を食べたことがある」 → ○「昨日、ご飯を食べた」.
To stress "not even once", use 「一度も〜たことがない」; not ✕「一度に行ったことがない」 (「一度に」 means "all at once").

daily.title: Making small talk with someone new
daily.description: Asking about someone's experiences to start a conversation.
daily.example: Have you ever had Japanese food?

daily.title: Recommending a movie to a friend
daily.description: 「が」 is dropped in casual speech.
daily.example: Have you seen this movie? It's really good.

daily.title: Remembering a trip
daily.description: Talking about a rare experience.
daily.example: I've been to Hokkaido only once.

work.title: Describing experience in an interview
work.description: Explaining past work experience.
work.example: I previously worked at a trading company.

work.title: Checking a team member's experience
work.description: Asking whether someone has done it before assigning a task.
work.example: Have you used this machine before?

etymology: Made of the past auxiliary 「た」 + the formal noun 「こと」 (事, "matter, fact") + the case particle 「が」 + the existential verb 「ある」. Literally "there exists the fact of having done ...", i.e. "to have the experience of ...". 「た」 comes from the classical perfective auxiliary 「たり」 (て + あり). 「こと」 is written with the kanji 「事」, but as a grammatical formal noun it is usually written in kana.
formation: 「〜たことがある」 = past 「た」 + the formal noun 「こと」 (thing, matter) + particle 「が」 + the existence verb 「ある」. First 「〜た」 packages a past action as "a thing", then you say "this thing exists (in my life)", which means "have the experience of..."; say it "doesn't exist (「ない」)" and it means "have never...". Because it treats the event as something worth bringing up, it isn't used for ordinary things like eating yesterday. Replace 「た」 with the dictionary form and what gets packaged is no longer a past event but "cases where one does...", so 「〜ることがある」 means "sometimes...".

similar.title: 〜ることがある (sometimes)
similar.explanation: Same origin (both are 「こと＋がある」), but it follows the dictionary form and means "sometimes..." (「たまに遅刻することがある」). It describes a current tendency, not a past experience.

similar.title: 〜ている
similar.explanation: The "experience / record" use of 「〜ている」 can also express past experience (「彼は二回優勝している」), mostly when stating a track record objectively; 「〜たことがある」 focuses on whether you have ever had that experience.

similar.title: 〜たためしがない
similar.explanation: Used only in the negative, stressing "never once", often with dissatisfaction or sarcasm (「彼が約束を守ったためしがない」); 「〜たことがない」 is a neutral statement.

meaning: “Before ...” The main action happens before another action or event.
connection: Verb dictionary form + まえに; noun + の + まえに; time expression + まえに

senses.label: Before an action
senses.meaning: The second action comes before the first. The verb before 「前に」 is always in dictionary form, even if the whole sentence is in the past.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + 前に (×寝た前に → ○寝る前に)
examples: I brush my teeth before going to bed.
Please close the windows before you go out.
Before coming to Japan, I studied a little Japanese.

senses.label: Before an event
senses.meaning: Follows nouns for actions or events, such as 食事, 試験, and 会議. Note that 「駅の前に」 means “in front of the station” (a place), which is a different use.
senses.connection: Action noun + の + 前に
examples: Let's wash our hands before eating.
Please read the materials before the meeting.

senses.label: (Time) ago
senses.meaning: After a length of time, it means “that long ago”, counting back from now. No 「の」 in between.
senses.connection: Time expression + 前に (三年前に, 10分前に)
examples: I came to Japan three years ago.
I arrived at the station 10 minutes ago.

notes: The verb before 「前に」 is always in the dictionary form, even when the whole sentence is about the past: ✕「日本に来た前に」 → ○「日本に来る前に勉強した」.
「前に」 only shows order, not a deadline. To require something to be done by a certain time, use 「までに」: ✕「明日の前にレポートを出してください」 → ○「明日までにレポートを出してください」.
「三年前に」 counts three years back from now; 「卒業の三年前に」 counts three years back from graduation. The reference point differs, and so does the meaning.

daily.title: Your bedtime routine
daily.description: Describing the order of your daily activities.
daily.example: I always read a little before going to sleep.

daily.title: Reminding family before going out
daily.description: Telling someone to do something first.
daily.example: Check the gas before you leave, okay?

daily.title: Taking photos before eating
daily.description: Talking about a little habit.
daily.example: I like to take a picture of my food before I eat.

work.title: Preparing for a meeting
work.description: Explaining the order of tasks.
work.example: I'll email the materials before the meeting.

work.title: Handing over work before a business trip
work.description: Planning what to finish before leaving.
work.example: I'll get my work wrapped up before I leave on my business trip.

etymology: 「まえ」 is written 「前」. Its origin is generally thought to be 「ま（目）」 (eye) + 「へ（方）」 (direction), i.e. "the direction the eyes face", originally meaning "in front" in space. It later extended from a spatial to a temporal meaning ("ahead of a certain moment"), giving the temporal use of 「〜前に」. This shift from space to time is common across languages; English "before" likewise originally meant "in front of" (as in "stand before the king").
formation: 「〜前に」 = verb dictionary form (or noun + の) + the noun 「前」 (front) + the time particle 「に」. 「前」 originally meant the space "in front". Picture time as a line, and the space in front of an event is the stretch before it happens, so 「寝る前に」 is "ahead of the event of sleeping". Since 「寝る」 hasn't happened yet at that point, the verb before it always takes the dictionary form, which expresses something not yet realized, even when the sentence is about the past. 「に」 places the following action within that stretch of time, so it only shows order and doesn't draw a cut-off line the way 「までに」 does.

similar.title: 〜までに
similar.explanation: Both relate to "before a certain time" and are very easy to confuse. 「前に」 gives the order of two events; 「までに」 gives a deadline, requiring completion by that point: 「5時までに来てください」.

similar.title: 〜うちに
similar.explanation: 「〜ないうちに」 is close in meaning to 「〜前に」 (「暗くならないうちに帰ろう」 ≈ 「暗くなる前に帰ろう」), but 「うちに」 stresses doing it quickly while the situation hasn't changed yet, with a sense of urgency; 「前に」 is just objective order.

similar.title: 〜の前・〜の上・〜の中 (position nouns)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「前」 is originally a spatial noun meaning "front" (「駅の前で待つ」), and the time meaning of 「〜前に」 developed from it. For position it means "in front of"; for time it means "before".

meaning: “After ...” The second action happens after the first one is finished.
connection: Verb ta-form + あとで; noun + の + あとで

senses.label: After an action
senses.meaning: One action is finished, then the next happens. The verb is always in ta-form, even when talking about the future. It only shows order; the second action doesn't have to follow right away.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + 後で (あとで)
examples: I'm going to the gym after work.
You can play games after you've done your homework.

senses.label: After an event
senses.meaning: Follows nouns for activities, such as 授業, 仕事, and 会議.
senses.connection: Noun + の + 後で
examples: Let's talk a bit after the meeting.
After class, I asked the teacher a question.

senses.label: Shortened forms and variants
senses.meaning: Dropping 「で」 gives 「〜た後、〜」, common in writing and news. 「〜た後に」 focuses on a point in time. 「〜た後は」 contrasts before and after.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + 後、／後に／後は
examples: After watching the movie, we ate at a restaurant.
After I graduate, I plan to work in my hometown.

notes: The verb before 「後で」 must be in the ta-form: ✕「食べる後で」 → ○「食べた後で」 (the exact opposite of 「前に」, which requires the dictionary form).
"Ever since..." can only be expressed with 「〜てから」: ✕「日本に来た後で、ずっと東京に住んでいる」 → ○「日本に来てから、ずっと東京に住んでいる」.
On its own, 「あとで」 means "later, in a bit" (「あとで電話します」). When a superior gives you a task, answering only 「あとでやります」 can sound like you're putting it off; it's better to give a specific time.

daily.title: Going for a walk after dinner
daily.description: Planning what to do and in what order.
daily.example: Let's go for a walk after we eat.

daily.title: A beer after a bath
daily.description: Talking about a moment you enjoy.
daily.example: Nothing beats a beer after a hot bath.

daily.title: Coffee after a movie with a friend
daily.description: Noun + の + 後で.
daily.example: Want to go to a café after the movie?

work.title: Reporting after a meeting
work.description: Explaining the order of tasks.
work.example: After the meeting ends, I'll report to the department manager.

work.title: A teacher calls a student in after class
work.description: Specifying a time.
work.example: Please come to the staff room after class.

etymology: 「あと」 is written 「後」 or 「跡」, originally meaning "footprint, trace"; it is generally considered cognate with 「跡」 (one theory derives it from 「あ（足）」 "foot" + 「と（処）」 "place"). From "the trace left after passing" it came to mean "behind" in space, and then "after" in time. 「で」 is a case particle marking a time frame or circumstance. 「〜た後で」 literally means "in the time after having done ...".
formation: 「〜た後で」 = past 「た」 (or noun + の) + the noun 「後」 (behind) + particle 「で」. 「後」 originally meant footprints or what lies behind; applied to time, it is "the period after an event". To be "behind" an event, that event must already have happened, so the verb before it always takes the ta-form, which expresses completion, in perfect symmetry with 「前に」 taking the dictionary form. 「で」 places the following action inside this "after" period and only conveys the time relationship, without the 「〜てから」 sense of "immediately after" or "as a prerequisite". Dropping 「で」, as in 「〜た後、」, is more formal.

similar.title: 〜てから
similar.explanation: 「〜てから」 stresses doing the next thing right after finishing one, or treats the first action as a prerequisite for the second; 「〜た後で」 is just the order in time. "Ever since..." can only be 「〜てから」.

similar.title: 〜上で
similar.explanation: 「〜た上で」 also means "after...", but stresses that the first action is a necessary prerequisite for the second, mostly in formal settings: 「よく考えた上で決めてください」.

similar.title: 〜たばかり
similar.explanation: 「〜たばかり」 stresses that an action was completed only a short while ago (it feels recent to the speaker); 「〜た後で」 only gives order, with no sense of "just now".

meaning: After the verb ます-stem it means “while doing ... (also) doing ...” (simultaneous actions or two activities carried on in parallel); it also expresses concession, “although ... yet ...”, and forms set phrases such as 「残念ながら」.
connection: Verb ます-stem + ながら; concessive: verb ている form, い-adjective dictionary form, な-adjective stem, or noun + ながら（も）

senses.label: Simultaneous actions
senses.meaning: One person does two things at once. The action before 「ながら」 is secondary; the one at the end of the sentence is the main action. The verb before it is usually one that continues over time.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + ながら (聞きます→聞きながら; 食べます→食べながら)
examples: I read the paper while drinking coffee.
My mother is singing as she cooks.
Please don't look at your phone while walking.

senses.label: Over a period of time
senses.meaning: Doing two things in parallel over a longer period, such as working while going to school.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + ながら
examples: I attend a Japanese language school while working part-time.
I study at university while working.

senses.label: Even though (one knows)
senses.meaning: The first part is an ongoing state or awareness, yet the person does something that contradicts it. It often carries blame, regret, or self-mockery. 「〜ていながら」 and 「〜でありながら」 are very common.
senses.connection: Verb te-iru form + ながら（も）／noun + でありながら（も）; common: 「知っていながら」, 「分かっていながら」, 「知りながら」
examples: He knew what was going on, yet he said nothing.
I know it's bad for me, but I still end up smoking.
Even though he's a doctor, he doesn't care about his own health.

senses.label: Although ... still
senses.meaning: The first part is a quality or attribute, and the second part is an evaluation that goes against it, as in “small but ...” or “only a child, but ...”. It sounds fairly literary and often takes 「も」.
senses.connection: i-adjective dictionary form／na-adjective stem／noun + ながら（も）; e.g. 「狭いながらも」, 「小さいながらも」, 「子供ながら」
examples: Our home: small, but full of joy.
This shop is small, but it's always packed with customers.
He's just a child, but he has a mind of his own.

senses.label: Set phrases
senses.meaning: Fixed expressions used to open politely or to sound modest. They are courteous and common in greetings and letters.
senses.connection: 「残念ながら」, 「失礼ながら」, 「恐縮ながら」, 「陰ながら」, 「微力ながら」, 「我ながら」, etc.
examples: Unfortunately, I can't take part this time.
Excuse me, but may I ask your name?
I'm rooting for you from the sidelines.

notes: Both actions must have the same subject; for different subjects, use 「〜間」: ✕「母が料理しながら、私はテレビを見た」 → ○「母が料理している間、私はテレビを見た」.
The main action goes after; what comes before 「ながら」 is the secondary action. In 「音楽を聞きながら勉強する」 the focus is on studying; swap them and the focus shifts too.

In Japan, looking at your phone while walking (「歩きスマホ」) or eating while walking is seen as bad manners; doing something else while a superior or client is talking (「〜しながら聞く」) is also considered disrespectful.

With an action verb, 「ます-stem＋ながら」 means “while doing ...” by default: 「テレビを見ながら勉強した」 is “studied while watching TV”, not “although I watched TV, I studied”. To express contrast, use 「〜ていながら（も）」 or add 「も」.
「生まれながら（に）」, 「昔ながらの」 and 「涙ながらに」 mean “as it is / with ...” and have no contrastive meaning, so do not translate them as “although”.

daily.title: Watching the news over breakfast
daily.description: Describing a daily habit.
daily.example: I watch the news while eating breakfast.

daily.title: Telling a child to focus
daily.description: A parent warns a child not to get distracted.
daily.example: No doing homework in front of the TV.

daily.title: Making fun of yourself to a friend
daily.description: You did it even though you knew you shouldn't, with a bit of self-mockery.
daily.example: I knew I was on a diet, but I ate the cake anyway.

daily.title: Describing your home
daily.description: Modestly saying your place is small but comfortable.
daily.example: It's small, but it's a cozy room.

daily.title: Turning down an invitation
daily.description: Politely saying you can't come.
daily.example: Unfortunately, I have plans that day.

work.title: Working and studying
work.description: Describing your current lifestyle.
work.example: I work during the day and go to vocational school at night.

work.title: Taking notes in a meeting
work.description: An instruction to staff or students.
work.example: Please take notes as you listen.

work.title: Thanking a client in a business email
work.description: Expressing modesty and support to a client.
work.example: I would be glad to help in whatever small way I can.

work.title: A news report about a company
work.description: Describing a company that is small but strong.
work.example: Although small, the company is known for its advanced technology.

etymology: 「ながら」 already existed in Classical Japanese. It is generally thought to come from the Old Japanese genitive particle 「な」 (equivalent to 「の」) + the noun 「から」 ("nature, original state, same condition", cognate with 「柄（がら）」), originally meaning "keeping the original state of ...", as in 「昔ながら」 (just as in the old days) and 「涙ながら」 (with tears). From "maintaining a state" it developed both the meaning "while an action continues" (simultaneity) and the contrastive meaning "although in a certain state, ...".
formation: 「ながら」is generally thought to come from the old attributive 「な」 plus 「から（柄）」, meaning “nature, manner”, so it originally meant “while remaining in the state of ...”. If you do B while remaining in state A, two things hold at once, which gives “while doing ... and ...”. When A should have prevented B but B happens anyway, “doing B while still in state A” turns into the contrastive “although A, B”. Adding 「も」 (“even”) stresses “even in state A ...” and makes the contrast clearer. Because the core idea is “remaining in a state”, the first part of the contrastive use is usually a stative word: 「〜ている」, 「ある」, an adjective, or a noun.

similar.title: 〜つつ
similar.explanation: Same meaning ("while...") and also has a contrastive use (「悪いと知りつつ」), but 「つつ」 is written language; in everyday conversation use 「ながら」.

similar.title: 〜間・〜間に
similar.explanation: 「間」 sets a period of time as the background, and the two clauses can have different subjects (「母が料理している間、私は…」); 「ながら」 is one person doing two things at the same time.

similar.title: 〜ものの
similar.explanation: 「ものの」 focuses on “that is true, but what should follow didn't”, and often follows the ta-form (「買ったものの、一度も使っていない」). 「ながらも」 focuses on the clash between state and action, or attribute and evaluation, in the same subject, and can follow adjectives and nouns.

meaning: “Because / since ...” Gives a cause or reason. More objective, softer, and politer than 「から」.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + ので; noun / na-adjective + なので; formal: 〜ますので／〜ですので

senses.label: Objective cause and effect
senses.meaning: Presents cause and effect as an objective fact. Common when explaining circumstances or natural results.
senses.connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + ので; noun / na-adjective + なので
examples: This road is narrow, so cars can't get through.
Tomorrow is Sunday, so there's no school.

senses.label: Polite reasons
senses.meaning: Used to give a reason to a superior or client when asking for time off, apologizing, or making a request. It sounds gentle rather than like an excuse.
senses.connection: Verb plain form + ので (followed by 「〜させてください」, 「〜いただけますか」, etc.)
examples: I have a fever, so please let me take today off.
I'm not feeling well. Would it be all right if I left early?

senses.label: Formal version
senses.meaning: In business, 「〜ますので」 and 「〜ですので」 are even more polite. Common in emails and notices.
senses.connection: Verb masu-form / です + ので
examples: I'll send you the materials, so please take a look.
I'll be on a business trip next week, so my replies may be delayed.

notes: Nouns and na-adjectives take 「なので」: ✕「雨だので」 → ○「雨なので」.
Following 「ので」 with a harsh command or prohibition sounds unnatural: ✕「危ないので触るな」 → ○「危ないから触るな」.
The spoken contraction 「〜んで」 (「時間ないんで」) sounds casual to clients and superiors; in formal settings say 「〜ので」 or 「〜ますので」.
Sentence-final 「〜のです」 and 「〜のでは」 are forms of 「のだ」, not the reason 「ので」: 「行くのです」 = (it's that) I'm going.

daily.title: Turning down a friend's invitation
daily.description: Giving a reason keeps it polite and gentle.
daily.example: Sorry, I have something on tomorrow, so I can't make it.

daily.title: Greeting neighbors before moving
daily.description: Politely explaining why you've come.
daily.example: We're moving next week, so we came to say goodbye.

daily.title: A sign on a shop door
daily.description: Stating the situation objectively.
daily.example: We are closed today for our regular holiday.

work.title: Calling in to take the day off
work.description: Give the reason first, then the request.
work.example: My child has a fever, so I'll be taking today off.

work.title: Explaining in a business email
work.description: 「〜ておりますので」 is more formal.
work.example: I'm out of the office today, so I'll get in touch tomorrow.

etymology: 「ので」 combines the nominalizing particle (formal noun) 「の」 with 「で」, the continuative form of the copula 「だ」; literally something like "it is the fact that ..., (so)". It is generally thought that this form began to be used as a conjunctive particle in the late Edo period and became widespread after the Meiji era. Because it explains a cause by nominalizing the preceding clause (「の」) and then asserting it, it feels more objective and softer than 「から」.
formation: 「ので」 = the nominalizing particle 「の」 + 「で」, the continuative form of the copula 「だ」. 「の」 first turns the whole preceding clause into a noun-like "fact", and 「で」 continues in the sense of "that being the case, ...". In other words, 「ので」 wraps the cause up as an objectively existing fact rather than the speaker's assertion, which is why it is more objective and gentler than 「から」. Because what comes before it is the noun-like 「の」, nouns and na-adjectives take the attributive 「な」 (「雨なので」), matching the structure of 「雨なのだ」.

similar.title: 〜から (reason)
similar.explanation: Both express reasons. 「から」 is subjective and can lead directly into commands or intentions; 「ので」 presents cause and effect as an objective fact with a gentle tone, suited to requests, apologies and business settings.

similar.title: 〜て・〜で (cause)
similar.explanation: 「〜て」 can also express a cause (「遅れてすみません」), but the causal link is looser, and it can't be followed by commands, requests or intentions: ✕「時間がなくて、急いでください」 → ○「時間がないので、急いでください」.

similar.title: 〜ものだから
similar.explanation: Also gives a reason, but with an excusing nuance of "it couldn't be helped" (「電車が遅れたものですから」), mostly used in apologies and explanations.

similar.title: 〜んです・〜のです
similar.explanation: Same origin: both 「ので」 and 「のです」 are built from 「の」 + the copula 「だ」. 「のです」 explains a situation at the end of a sentence; 「ので」 links a reason in the middle of a sentence.

meaning: “Want (something).” Expresses the speaker's desire for a thing.
connection: Noun + が + ほしい (欲しい); conjugates like an i-adjective

senses.label: Wanting something
senses.meaning: You want a certain thing. Use it only for yourself, or in questions to the listener.
senses.connection: Noun + が + ほしい／ほしいです
examples: I want a new computer.
What do you want for your birthday?

senses.label: Not wanting
senses.meaning: The negative 「ほしくない」 means you don't want or need it. In negatives and contrasts, 「が」 often becomes 「は」 or 「も」.
senses.connection: Noun + は／も + ほしくない
examples: I don't want anything right now.
I don't want a car.

senses.label: Wanted (past)
senses.meaning: 「ほしかった」 is a past wish, often with nostalgia or regret.
senses.connection: Noun + が + ほしかった
examples: When I was a kid, I wanted a dog.
I've wanted this bag for ages.

senses.label: Someone else wants
senses.meaning: For a third person's wishes, use 「ほしがる」, usually as 「ほしがっている」. The object then takes 「を」.
senses.connection: Noun + を + ほしがる／ほしがっている
examples: My little brother wants a new game.
The child is crying because he wants a toy.

notes: 「ほしい」 can only be said directly about yourself (or asked of the listener). For someone else use 「ほしがる」, and the particle changes to 「を」: ✕「妹は人形がほしい」 → ○「妹は人形をほしがっている」.
Asking a superior or client 「何が欲しいですか」 or 「コーヒーが欲しいですか」 is rude, as if prying into their desires; say 「何になさいますか」 or 「コーヒーはいかがですか」 instead.
The thing you want is marked with 「が」: ✕「パソコンをほしい」 → ○「パソコンがほしい」.

「〜がほしい」 follows a noun (wanting a thing); 「〜てほしい」 follows the te-form (wanting someone else to do something). The targets are completely different: 「手伝いがほしい」 vs 「手伝ってほしい」. The latter is usually written in kana, 「ほしい」.

daily.title: Asking a friend about a gift
daily.description: Friends ask each other directly.
daily.example: What do you want for your birthday?

daily.title: Spotting clothes you love while shopping
daily.description: Expressing a strong desire.
daily.example: I really want this dress!

daily.title: Wishing for a pet
daily.description: 「なあ」 at the end adds a wistful tone.
daily.example: I wish I had a cat.

work.title: Asking a teacher or boss for more time
work.description: Stating what you need in a fairly soft way.
work.example: I'd like a little more time.

work.title: Chatting with coworkers about equipment
work.description: Fine among coworkers. When asking a superior what they want, use 「ご希望」 instead.
work.example: It'd be nice to have a bigger monitor, wouldn't it?

etymology: 「ほしい」 comes from the Classical Japanese adjective 「ほし」 (欲し, shiku-type conjugation), cognate with the old verb 「ほる」 (欲る, "to want"). The attributive form 「ほしき」 became 「ほしい」 through i-onbin. It is written 「欲しい」 in kanji, but as an auxiliary adjective (〜てほしい) it is usually written in kana.
formation: 「〜がほしい」 = noun + particle 「が」 + the emotive adjective 「ほしい（欲しい）」. Like 「うれしい」 and 「こわい」, 「ほしい」 is an adjective describing the speaker's inner feeling, and 「が」 marks the object that causes that feeling, which is why you say 「パソコンがほしい」 and not 「を」. Being an adjective, it conjugates like an i-adjective (「ほしくない」, 「ほしかった」); being an inner feeling, it can only be said directly about yourself. For other people, adding 「がる」 (to show signs of) turns it into the verb 「ほしがる」; the thing wanted becomes the verb's object, and the particle changes to 「を」 accordingly.

similar.title: 〜たい
similar.explanation: 「ほしい」 means wanting a thing and follows a noun; 「〜たい」 means wanting to do an action and follows a verb: ○「車がほしい」／○「車を買いたい」, not ✕「車を買いほしい」.

similar.title: 〜てほしい・〜てもらいたい
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「ほしい」 after the te-form expresses wanting someone else to do something (「早く元気になってほしい」). What you want is no longer a thing but another person's action.

similar.title: 〜がる・〜がっている
similar.explanation: 「ほしい」 is only for yourself; for a third person use 「ほしがる」: 「子どもがおもちゃをほしがっている」, and the particle changes from 「が」 to 「を」.

meaning: “Intend to / plan to ...” A plan decided in advance. It can also mean “thought I had ...” or “meant it as ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + つもりだ; verb ta-form / noun + の + つもり

senses.label: Intend to do
senses.meaning: A plan you have thought about and are fairly sure of. More planned than 「〜たい」 and more firm than 「〜(よ)うと思う」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + つもりだ
examples: I plan to study abroad in Japan next year.
I'm planning to go back to my home country for summer vacation.

senses.label: Not intending to
senses.meaning: There are two negatives. 「〜ないつもりだ」 means you intend not to do it. 「〜つもりはない」 means you have no such intention at all, which is stronger.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + つもりだ; verb dictionary form + つもりはない
examples: I intend never to smoke again.
I have no intention of joining that company.

senses.label: Thought I had
senses.meaning: Ta-form + 「つもり」 means you believed you did something, but in reality you didn't. Often 「〜つもりだったが」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + つもり(だった)
examples: I thought I'd locked it, but it was open.
I thought I'd explained it well. Was it hard to follow?

senses.label: Meant as / treat as
senses.meaning: Noun + の + 「つもり」 means treating something as something else, or explains what you really meant.
senses.connection: Noun + の + つもり
examples: I only meant it as a joke.
I enjoyed the business trip as if it were a vacation.

notes: Asking a superior or client 「〜つもりですか」 directly sounds like you're interrogating their intentions, which is rude; ask 「〜ご予定ですか」 or 「〜なさいますか」 instead.
「どういうつもりですか」 and 「どういうつもりだ」 are accusations ("What on earth do you mean by this?"), not simple questions.
Negatives differ in strength: 「行かないつもりだ」 = I plan not to go; 「行くつもりはない」 = I have no intention whatsoever of going, a firm and explicit refusal.
Ta-form + つもり means "thought I had... (but actually didn't)", not "plan to": 「鍵をかけたつもりだった」 = I thought I had locked the door (but I hadn't).
For business matters already on the schedule, use 「予定」; at work 「〜つもりです」 only expresses a personal intention and sounds less certain.

daily.title: Chatting about weekend plans
daily.description: Telling a friend what you plan to do.
daily.example: I'm planning to just relax at home this weekend.

daily.title: New Year's resolutions
daily.description: Stating your determination.
daily.example: This year I'm really going to quit drinking.

daily.title: Apologizing to a friend
daily.description: Explaining that it wasn't on purpose.
daily.example: Sorry, I didn't mean to make you angry.

work.title: Stating your commitment in an interview
work.description: Expressing a long-term plan.
work.example: I intend to work at your company for a long time.

work.title: Asked about changing jobs
work.description: 「つもりはない」 makes your position clear.
work.example: For now, I have no plans to change jobs.

etymology: 「つもり」 is the nominalized continuative form of the verb 「積もる」 (つもる, "to pile up", extended to "to estimate, to calculate"). Written 「積もり」 or 「積り」, it originally meant "estimate, budget", a sense still preserved in 「見積もり」 (quotation, estimate). From "estimating in advance" it came to mean "one's inner calculation, intention". 「心算」 is a borrowed-kanji spelling for this meaning; today it is generally written in kana as 「つもり」.
formation: 「つもり」 is the noun form of the verb 「積もる」 (to pile up → to estimate), originally meaning "an estimate, a calculation in one's mind". Dictionary form + つもり is "a calculation about doing... in the future", that is, an intention; ta-form + つもり is "being convinced in one's mind that one has done...", and since a mental calculation doesn't always match reality, it comes to mean "thought one had". Noun + の + つもり is "treating it in one's mind as...". All three uses come from the core idea of "a calculation in one's mind", which is why 「つもり」 is more personal and subjective than 「予定」.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うと思う
similar.explanation: 「〜(よ)うと思う」 often expresses a decision made at the moment of speaking; 「つもり」 expresses a firmer plan already thought out beforehand.

similar.title: 〜予定だ
similar.explanation: 「予定」 is an objectively arranged schedule (including ones decided by your company or others); 「つもり」 is a personal intention in your own mind. Use 「予定」 for flights, meetings and the like.

similar.title: 〜ことにする
similar.explanation: 「〜ことにする」 stresses the act of making a decision (「留学することにした」); 「つもり」 just states the intention in your mind, without focusing on the moment of deciding.

similar.title: 〜たつもり
similar.explanation: Same origin: after the ta-form it means "believed one had already...", contrary to fact (「わかったつもりでいた」), not "plan to".

meaning: “You'd better / you should ...” Gives advice or a warning. The negative means “you'd better not ...”.
connection: Verb ta-form + ほうがいい; verb nai-form + ほうがいい

senses.label: Advising to do
senses.meaning: Recommends doing something. The ta-form is the norm and sounds fairly clear. Politely: 「〜たほうがいいですよ」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ほうがいい (方がいい)
examples: You look pale. You should go to bed early tonight.
You really should quit smoking.

senses.label: Advising not to
senses.meaning: Recommends not doing something. Use the nai-form; ×なかったほうがいい is wrong.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ほうがいい
examples: You'd better not walk alone at night.
You shouldn't drink unboiled water.

senses.label: Regret
senses.meaning: 「〜たほうがよかった」 expresses regret: “I should have ...”.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ほうがよかった
examples: We should have left earlier.
I should have brought an umbrella.

senses.label: General advice
senses.meaning: With the dictionary form, it leans toward general truths or comparisons, not advice for a specific situation.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ほうがいい
examples: It's better to study a foreign language a little every day.

notes: Saying 「〜たほうがいいですよ」 to a superior or client sounds like you're instructing them, which is rude; use 「〜てはいかがでしょうか」 or 「〜たほうがよろしいかと存じます」 instead.
For negative advice, use the nai-form + ほうがいい: ✕「行かなかったほうがいい」 → ○「行かないほうがいい」.
「〜たほうがよかった」 expresses regret or blame ("I/you should have..."); said to others it sounds critical: 「もっと早く言ったほうがよかったね」.
Noun + のほうがいい compares two options and states a preference (「紅茶のほうがいい」); it is not advice.

daily.title: A friend has a cold
daily.description: Showing concern and giving advice.
daily.example: If you have a fever, you should go to the doctor.

daily.title: Tips for a tourist
daily.description: Sharing experience and making a suggestion.
daily.example: Kyoto gets crowded, so it's best to go early in the morning.

daily.title: Talking a friend out of going
daily.description: Advising against something.
daily.example: That place is expensive, so I wouldn't go there.

work.title: A senior advising a junior
work.description: Fine to use directly with juniors.
work.example: It's a good idea to double-check important emails before sending them.

work.title: A gentle suggestion to your boss
work.description: With superiors, adding 「〜かと思います」 softens it.
work.example: I think it might be best to book the venue in advance.

etymology: 「ほう」 is written 「方」, originally meaning "direction, side", and by extension "one side" of two alternatives. 「〜ほうがいい」 literally means "the side of (doing ...) is better". It was originally a comparative expression (AよりBのほうがいい); the item being compared was later omitted, and it became a fixed pattern for giving advice. 「いい」 is the colloquial form of 「よい」, so its past tense is 「よかった」.
formation: 「〜ほうがいい」 = verb (ta-form / nai-form) + the noun 「方（ほう）」 (one side of two) + 「が」 + 「いい」. Literally: "the side (of doing...) is good". Underneath it is the comparative sentence 「AよりBのほうがいい」: the speaker compares doing and not doing and names the better side, which becomes advice. The side not chosen is implied to be "not good", so it sounds stronger than a simple suggestion and often implies "or you'll be in trouble". Turn 「いい」 into the past 「よかった」 and you are evaluating a choice already made, which expresses regret or blame.

similar.title: 〜たらどうですか
similar.explanation: Both make suggestions. 「〜たらどうですか」 suggests in the form of a question, lighter and leaving room to say no; 「〜ほうがいい」 states flatly that this is better, with a stronger advisory tone.

similar.title: 〜べきだ
similar.explanation: 「べきだ」 argues from reason or duty that something "should" be done and is firmer than 「ほうがいい」; 「ほうがいい」 judges from pros and cons that "this is better for you".

similar.title: 〜ばいい
similar.explanation: 「〜ばいい」 tells the listener a method, "all you need to do is..." (「駅で聞けばいい」), used to answer "What should I do?"; 「〜ほうがいい」 recommends one option after comparing.

similar.title: 〜より〜のほうが
similar.explanation: Same origin: it comes from the comparative sentence 「AよりBのほうがいい」; when the thing being compared is left out, it turns into the advice-giving 「〜ほうがいい」.
